description: We are a two-person team participating in NASA Space Apps. We are interested in exploring how satellite data and technology can help detect wildfires and share useful information with communities. For this challenge, we hope to contribute ideas and develop a clear, practical proposal to improve wildfire prevention and response.
summary:
FireWatch Paraguay is a web app that turns NASA FIRMS thermal detections into a map and a monthly calendar for Paraguay. We processed about 3 million MODIS and VIIRS detections from 2000 to 2026, and for any month you can see how it compares with the same month in earlier years.

MODIS and VIIRS can’t be compared directly, so we tested a seasonal scaling factor between them. It gives one continuous series, still experimental, with each sensor’s original counts shown alongside. The app also lets you explore where detections cluster, filter by department, and look at recent data.

This matters because raw satellite detections are hard to place in local and seasonal context. FireWatch helps researchers, land managers and emergency teams spot months that stand out and decide where to look closer. It is not a forecast or an alert system, and a FIRMS detection is a thermal anomaly, not a confirmed fire.
details:
FireWatch Paraguay is a web app for exploring 26 years of NASA FIRMS thermal detections in a local context. We worked with four official FIRMS files for Paraguay: 2,973,595 detections from November 1, 2000 to November 5, 2026 (MODIS) and November 1, 2026 (VIIRS). MODIS starts in 2000 and VIIRS in 2012, and the two can’t simply be added together because they differ in resolution, sensitivity and overpass time.

The History tab is a monthly calendar. When you pick a month, the app compares it with the same month in earlier years and shows the median, the P10–P90 range and how many years it is based on. We also built an experimental combined series. Before 2012 it uses MODIS only. Where both sensors overlap, it averages MODIS with VIIRS scaled by a seasonal factor. Recent near-real-time months are marked as provisional, and the original counts for each sensor stay visible next to it. As an example, January 2022 comes to about 8,982 in the combined series, against a median of 1,703 and a P90 of 2,513 for the 21 previous Januaries.

To check the scaling, we ran a forward-looking test over 78 months (February 2020 to July 2026), where each month was estimated using only earlier data. Compared with MODIS counts, the seasonal factor gave a 10.6% error (WAPE), a single factor gave 11.1%, and no scaling gave 250.7%. That only tells us how well VIIRS matches MODIS. It is not ground truth, so we still call the series experimental.

The Map tab and the spatial-pattern tools show where detections cluster and where they keep coming back, and you can select cities or draw areas. A slider lets you compare a clean basemap with the detections on top. The Recent Data tab queries NASA FIRMS for MODIS and VIIRS with sensor and time filters, daily summaries, clusters and CSV export. National historical totals keep every detection. Department views use the 2012 reference boundaries, so 8,528 detections (0.29%) that fall outside that layer and 31 that sit on a boundary are left unassigned.

We think this can help researchers, land managers and emergency teams see how a month compares with the past and decide where a closer look is worth it. It is not a forecast or an alert system, and a FIRMS detection is a thermal anomaly, not a confirmed fire. It can be agricultural burning or another heat source.

The app is built with React, JavaScript, Vite, Leaflet and Recharts, with Node.js scripts to process the source files. A small Node.js proxy keeps our FIRMS API key on the server. The code is on GitHub and the app is hosted on Render. It runs in a browser and needs no special hardware. Throughout, we tried to avoid overselling the data: we kept both sensors visible instead of merging them quietly, marked incomplete and provisional periods, and did not present detections as confirmed incidents.
